newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW-Australia Sept c/a data.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW-Australia Sept c/a data.

text.p: Australia's seasonally adjusted current account deficit came in at A$1.69 billion in September, after revisions, well above forecasts which centred on a deficit of A$1.3 billion. The August deficit was A$1.47 billion.
The following is a selection of economists' early reactions to the data.
HELEN CAMP, SENIOR ECONOMIST, WESTPAC BANKING CORP:

"Certainly this was a big surprise. We would want to see a few months data to assess the net income deficit deterioration, which doesn't seem to gel with our forecasts, certainly in terms of a relatively solid Australian dollar over the quarter. But the exports seem to have been underperforming a little. Westpac is still looking for a cyclical improvement in the current account deficit, largely due to an improvement in the trade balance over the course of this year."

"Obviously it was a worse than expected result due to a decline in exports and it appears that was primarily on the rural side. The widening of the net income deficit surprised me a little, it normally doesn't move around that much. I would say this data has virtually a zero implication for rates. In terms of the GDP outlook, it means the positive contribution that you were going to get from net exports is going to be a little bit less because it looks like export volumes did not rise by as much as we had expected in the quarter. So that means we might be looking at a slightly lower GDP estimate than people had thought before these numbers."
ROB HENDERSON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, DRESDNER INTERNATIONAL:

"The major change here is the change in the net trade balance which is going into a deficit after a surplus for a couple of months. We already knew that imports had risen slightly by one percent but what we didn't know was that exports had fallen by three percent. So the new bit of information today is exports. The knee-jerk reaction by the markets seemed to be based the view that it is a stronger economy and sucking in more imports. But actually when you look at it the new bit of news today is that exports were weak so if you were a policymaker concerned about the growth of the economy and growth in jobs these numbers are more reason to worry than you had before they came out."
ANDREW PEASE, SENIOR ECONOMIST, NOMURA RESEARCH AUSTRALIA:

"Overall it is very hard to make any sort of analysis of these numbers just because of the extent of the revisions. The fact that we did get a A$1.7 billion deficit was due to the higher basis than we were expecting, leaving the market pretty much in the dark about what these numbers would be. It certainly not a number I would be worrying about just yet. Monthly current account deficits are a dead issue at the moment."
